translation:
...people of the world have gone astray.

_Ganga bharose Jivana, bhulyo sab sansar,_
_Ja charanse upni, so samaryo nahi ekvar. ||2||_
(Trusting in the Ganga, O Jivan, the whole world has gone astray; but the One from whose feet she truly sprang, that Lord's remembrance they have not performed even once.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: out of the false belief that serving the Ganga will bring about our deliverance, all the people of the world have gone astray. But the Lord from whose feet the Ganga actually arose — his remembrance and devotion they have not performed even a single time. So how, then, will their deliverance ever come about?

_Jahan ki tahan tal jaigi, Ganga ujal dhar,_
_Ramnam bin Jivana, koi na pahoncha par. ||3||_
(The Ganga's bright stream will sink back to the place it came from; without the name of Ram, O Jivan, no one has ever crossed over.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: the bright stream of the Ganga will go back to the place from which it came. Without devotion to the name of Ram, no one will ever be able to cross the ocean of worldly existence.

_Ganga (Kashi) pali Kailaskun, triveni gai trut,_
_Kaliyugma Jivana, bhai Ramnamki lut. ||4||_
(The Ganga of Kashi will return to Kailas, and the confluence of the three rivers will come apart; in the Kali age, O Jivan, only the freely-taken plunder of Ram's name remains.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: when the power of the Ganga (of Kashi) ceases, she will dissolve back into her original abode, Kailas, and the confluence of the three rivers will come apart. But in the time of the Kali age, whatever joy each soul can gather from singing and remembering the name of Ram, that much will be freely taken and enjoyed.

_Bhajiko pani Jivana, aiso Gangako nir,_
_Lakshman sahit sang Janki, jake rude Raghuvir. ||5||_
(Like the watery liquid squeezed from cooked greens, so is the water of the Ganga, O Jivan; but in whose heart, together with Lakshman and Janaki, dwells the hero of Raghu's line —)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: just as the water squeezed out of cooked greens is a worthless, sapless liquid, so too is the water of the Ganga worthless and beneath reckoning. But whoever holds devotion to Ram within their heart — in them dwells Ram together with Sita and Lakshman.

_Kabir tirath vrat vakh veladi, rahi choho jug chhay,_
_Kabire mul nikandiya, kon halahal khay. ||6||_
(Kabir says: the creeper of pilgrimage and vows is a poison-vine that has cast its shade over all four ages; Kabir has torn it out by the root — who now would eat that deadly poison?)

Das Kabirji says: the poisonous creeper of pilgrimages and vows — a vine spreading the poison that casts people into the hell of desire and craving — has spread its tendrils and covered every corner in every age. But the true Guru, Kabir, has torn out this creeper of pilgrimage, vows, and mantras by its very root and thrown it away — that is, he has made people give up pilgrimages and vows entirely. So then, why should anyone fall into the trap of hell laid by this creeper of pilgrimage and vows, a creeper that has already been completely uprooted and destroyed?

This sakhi of Kabirji has been presented here in the Samagam a second time; it was also given earlier in the chapter "The Word Alone Is God." Thus, in this present chapter on the Honest-Looking Thief, while discussing the Ganga, Ekadashi, and other pilgrimage places, the Samagam strongly urges us to keep our distance from pilgrimages and vows — the very things Kabirji so firmly opposed.

_Ganga chali Kailaskun, jahan Gauri patiko dham,_
_Prithvi pavan bhai Jivana, rahyo Ramko nam. ||7||_
(The Ganga has departed for Kailas, the abode of Gauri's husband; the earth, O Jivan, has become pure, and only the name of Ram remains.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: since the Ganga has lost her potency and returned to Kailas, the abode of Shiva, husband of Parvati, that leftover water of the Ganga has left the earth, and so the earth has become pure; and now we have gained the benefit of practising unblemished devotion to the divine name, Ram.

_Ganga bharose Jivana, gayo janmaro bans,_
_Sitapati Raghunathkun, sapne nahi awaz. ||8||_
(Trusting in the Ganga, O Jivan, one's whole life is wasted; not even in a dream does one utter the name of Ram, the husband of Sita.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: the Ganga is held to purify even the fallen, and out of trust in this, people spend their lives serving her — and so their entire human birth is wasted, because, obsessed with the Ganga and endlessly chanting "Har Har Ganga," they never even dreamed of chanting the name of Ram, husband of Sita, in devotion.

_Vishnu padodak leyanta, akal mrityu mit jay,_
_Sant taranamrit le Jivana, akhe parampad pay. ||9||_
(By taking the water that has washed Vishnu's feet, only an untimely death is averted; but by taking the saving nectar from a saint's feet, O Jivan, one attains that very highest, imperishable state.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: drinking the water of the Ganga, said to be the nectar of Vishnu's feet, only wards off an untimely death; but drinking the nectar of a true saint's feet lets one attain that supreme, imperishable abode of the Lord.

_Ganga papam shashi tapam dainyam kalpatarusttha,_
_Papam tapam cha dainyam cha haret sajjanasangamah._
(The Ganga removes sin, the moon removes the heat of affliction, the wish-granting tree removes poverty — but the company of good people removes sin, affliction, and poverty, all three.)

The Ganga removes sin, the moon removes the heat of affliction, the wish-granting tree removes poverty — but the company of good people removes sin, affliction, and poverty, all together.

(A rekhta — manuscript ref.: Handwritten ms. no. 6, p. 77; Rekhta 61; Handwritten ms. no. 33, p. 146 verso:)

_Gang ulti dharo, Jamun bas karo, palat pand tirathi pap jave,_
_Nir niramal tihan raindin farat hai, nahai jyon bahudi bhav sindhu na nahave,_
_Firat bare tihan buddhiko nash hai, bajhke bhatakane sidh nahin,_
_Kabat Kabir is juktiku gahega, janam aur maran tab ant yanhi._
(Turn your inclination away from the Ganga and take up dwelling with the Yamuna; by that turning the sins clinging to the body from pilgrimage-chasing will depart. Her pure water flows there day and night; bathe in it once, and you need never bathe again in the ocean of worldly existence. Wandering elsewhere, outside of it, only destroys one's discernment — roaming about fruitlessly brings no accomplishment. Kabir says: whoever grasps this secret — for them birth and death will then come to an end.)

Das Kabirji says: turn away from your attachment to the Ganga, give it up, and instead cultivate devotion to the Yamuna. Householders commit five kinds of sin every day, unknowingly, through five household implements — the hearth, the grinding-stone, the broom, the pounding-mortar, and the water-jar — since living creatures die in the course of using them, knowingly or not; these are counted as the five sins. This pure water of the Yamuna, flowing there day and night, washes all five of these sins away. Immerse yourself fully in it, delight in it, bathe there, so that you need not wander about bathing elsewhere in the ocean of worldly existence. Wandering about outside of it will bring no success. Kabirji says: whoever grasps this secret, for them birth and death will then come to an end.

(Another rekhta — ref.: Nagarno-45, p. 49; Handwritten ms. no. 33, p. 147 verso; Handwritten ms. no. 6, p. 77:)

_Gang aru Jamnake ghatko khojale, bhaivar gunjar tahan karat bhai,_
_Saraswati nir tahan dekh nirmal vahe, tarake nir piye pyas jai,_
_Panchki pyas tahan dekh puri bhai, tinki tap tahan lage nahin,_
_Kahat Kabir yah agamka khel hai, gaibka chandana dekh manhi._
(Search out the true landing-ghat among those of the Ganga and the Yamuna — there, brother, the bee-like restless souls hum and swarm. See there the pure water of Saraswati flowing; drink of that saving water and your thirst departs. There the thirst of the five senses is fully quenched, and the three kinds of affliction never touch you. Kabir says: this is the play of the unfathomable — behold within it the moonlight of the unseen.)

Das Kabirji says: there are two kinds of ghats — of the Ganga and of the Yamuna. Of these, there is one ghat by which one truly crosses the ocean of worldly existence, and another that does not. So, of these two kinds of ghats, seek out and choose the Yamuna-like ghat — the one that carries us across the ocean of existence and brings about our deliverance. O brother! At this place, souls that wander detached like true saints, and other souls that wander caught up in sense-desires, both hum and gather there like bees. There flows the pure water of Saraswati — that is, the water of our own power of understanding. Drinking this water, which grants right understanding, causes the thirst of hope and craving, along with sin, to depart, and thus you will see that the five kinds of sensory affliction vanish. Moreover, the three kinds of affliction no longer touch you either. Kabirji says: this is the play of a profound, hidden truth; within it one catches a glimpse of the unseen, deeply hidden reality of God.

The Samagam explains that the name of the Sanakadi sages comes from the word "san," meaning austerity. This is mentioned in the fifth verse of the seventh chapter of the second canto of the Bhagavat, where it is said: "In the beginning of creation, out of the desire to bring the world into being, I performed unbroken austerity. Being pleased with that, I took birth in the forms of Sanaka, Sanandan, Sanatan, and Sanatkumar, bearing the mark of the name 'san,' meaning austerity." (Registration no. 2149, p. 172)

_Dharmambho Manikarnika Bhagavatah padambu Bhagirathi_
_Kashinamyati-ardham eva bhajate Shri Vishvanathah svayam,_
_Etasyaiva hi nama Shambhunagare nistarakam tarakam_
_Tasmat Krishnapadambujam bhaja sakhe Shripadnirvanadam._
(Registration no. 414, p. 375)

That is: from the water of whose sweat Manikarnika arose; from the water of whose feet the blessed Bhagirathi sprang; the Lord of Kashi himself, Shri Vishvanath, forms one half of whose own body — and in the city of Shiva, it is that name alone which has the power to ferry souls across the ocean of worldly existence. O friend, why then do you not worship the lotus feet of that liberation-granting Shri Krishna? — that is, meditate on those very lotus feet. This verse gives supreme importance to devotion, and shows liberation itself to be trivial beside it.

At Manikarnika, the priests harass people over the shraddha rites for ancestors. On this, the Bhagavad Gomandal (1986 edition), page 892, writes: after bathing in the Ganga, the priests conduct the shraddha rite, and in the process they grab and pull at the patron, defiling this sacred act through their harassment — a disgrace never to be forgotten. The time has come for a thorough reform of this custom. Kabirji indeed called shraddha nothing but hypocrisy.

Shrimad Bhagavat, Maha, chapter 1, verse 72, says:

_Atyugrabharikarmano, nastika raurava janah,_
_Te'pi nichchhanti tirtheshu, tirthasarastato gatah. ||72||_
(People who commit extremely terrible deeds, atheists, and those of a cruel, dreadful nature also come to settle at pilgrimage sites; because of this, the true essence of the pilgrimage sites has departed.)

People who commit extremely terrible deeds, atheists, and those of a cruel nature settle at places of pilgrimage; because of this the true essence of the pilgrimage sites has departed. So says Naradji at the beginning of the Kali age.

In the Ganga Sahasranama, the 622nd name of the Ganga is "Parameshthikamandalu" — meaning she who dwells in Brahma's kamandal (water-pot). Her 187th name is "Kutastha" — meaning she is of the very nature of Brahman. Thus the Samagam's account is confirmed: that Brahma caught the sweat of the Sanakadi sages in his kamandal, and this became the Ganga.

The dictionary defines "Brahmadrav" (Brahma-fluid) as Ganga water. In explaining the Ganga's names, the Ganga Sahasranama calls her "of the nature of Brahma-fluid." As we have seen, Kabirji told us to choose, of the two ghats of Ganga and Yamuna, whichever one brings about our deliverance. The Ganga's is a path of ritual observance, while the Yamuna's is a path of loving devotion; therefore he told us to accept the Yamuna's ghat — the current of loving devotion. In the Bhaktamal of the Vaikuntheshwar Press, pages 119-120, the glory of Yamunaji is sung at great length, and in it one kavit discusses and compares both the Ganga and the Yamuna.

_Brahmake kamandulute Girija prachandnate Shivajata mandanate dhariyon bahati hai,_
_Tino lok pavanko apda nashavanko jake gungavanko vani yon chahat hai,_
_Kahai kavirai sur asurah pujai jahi Surdhani kahai dukh pap na rahat hai,_
_Yamunajiki mahima yate na kahi pare Gangapagpani taki patrani kahat hai. ||4||_
(Falling with tremendous force from Brahma's kamandal, held in Shiva's matted locks — thus flows this current, sanctifying all three worlds and destroying calamity, whose praise the very voice longs to sing. The poet-king says: gods and demons alike worship her, calling her the celestial river and saying that through her, sin and sorrow depart. Yet Yamunaji's glory cannot even be told through her — for this Ganga is but the water of Yamuna's feet; Yamuna, they say, is her queen.)

Six kavits have been written in praise of the Yamuna; in this, the fourth, the Yamuna is declared superior to the Ganga. The poet says: falling with tremendous force from Brahma's kamandal, held in Shiva's matted locks, her current flows on, sanctifying all three worlds and destroying calamities — one whose praises the very voice longs to sing. Of her the poet-king says: such a heavenly river is worshipped by all, and it is said that worshipping her removes the suffering of sin. But even they cannot express the glory of Yamunaji — for, they say, this Ganga is not even equal to the water that has washed Yamunaji's feet; Yamunaji herself, they say, is the chief queen.

Dayaldas writes that the sweat of the Sanakadi sages, sons of Brahma, which was collected in Brahma's kamandal, spilled out when the Lord's foot struck it, and thus the Ganga appeared. (No. 36, p. 57)

_Dayala Brahmake sut char hai, taka angki sit,_
_So gaganse Ganga nikasi, phodi parbat bhint. ||1||_
(Dayaldas says: Brahma has four sons; from the moisture of their bodies, the Ganga issued forth from the sky, breaking through the mountain wall.)

Dayaldas says: Brahma's four sons, the Sanakadi sages, had a certain moisture from their bodies; from that, the Ganga issued forth from the sky, breaking through the mountain's wall.

The Vaishnav Dharma Ratnakar, page 17, states in a verse how long the Ganga's lifespan will be; going by this, the Ganga's lifespan may be reckoned as already having ended at present. And indeed, even today sewers are emptied into the Ganga, and hides are washed in her, so she has already become corrupted.

_Kalau dashasahastreshu Haristyajati medinim,_
_Tadardha Jahnavitoyam tadardha gramadevata. ||43||_
(Vaishnav Dharma Ratnakar, p. 17)

After ten thousand years of the Kali age have passed, the Lord will abandon this earth and go to Vaikuntha; after five thousand years of the Kali age have passed, Gangaji will abandon this earth; and after two-and-a-half thousand years of the Kali age have passed, the village deities who protect the villages will abandon this earth.

Kalyan, Year 8, Issue 10, Registration no. 19, page 1257, writes that these statements confirm what the Reva Purana says — that after five thousand years of the Kali age have passed, that is, around the year 1895 CE, the glory of Shri Gangaji will diminish.

Vrataraj, Registration no. 874, pages 345-346, states, in the 35th verse of the Kartik Mahatmya of the Vaikuntha Chaturdashi section of the Sanatkumar Samhita, that a person who worships Shankar without first worshipping Vishnu — his worship goes to waste. "This I say in all truth" — saying this much, Shankar disappeared.

Verses 37-38 say that when the fierce Kali age arrives and right conduct and thought are destroyed, then, after twenty-four hundred years, Mahadev will take all the lingas that exist in Kashi and go to the netherworld. Verses 39-40 say that, forty-eight hundred years after that, the Ganga and Kashi too will go to their own abode. When Kashi disappears, the marks of the lingas will also be destroyed, and all human beings will lose their vitality.

In V.S. 2033-34, Jivanvani, Year 2, Issue 10-11, page 3, Mohan Bhatt writes, in the Padmanabh Akhyan:

_Kali adyanan dash sahastra varsh, paryant pavan param,_
_Tehanu ardha rahese Jahnavi, Hari bhakti ne satkarm. ||4||_
(For the first ten thousand years of the Kali age, supreme purity will remain; for half of that period, the Jahnavi, devotion to Hari, and righteous conduct will remain.)

For the first half of the ten thousand years at the start of the Kali age, the Ganga will remain very pure, and devotion to Hari and righteous conduct will remain.

Reckoning by this count, the glory of Gangaji today would be considered already exhausted — and indeed this is truly the state to which Gangaji has come today: people empty sewers into the Ganga, and in Kanpur hides are washed in her. Moreover, Gangaji herself has grown fearful of these wicked people.

The Skanda Purana, Kashikhand, chapter 6, verse 55, says:

_Pardar pardravya pardroh parangmukhah,_
_Ganga bute kada agatya, mamayam pavayishyati. ||95||_
(The river Ganga says: a man free of desire for another's wife, another's wealth, and enmity toward others — when will such a man come and purify me?)

The river Ganga says: when will a man free of desire for another's wife, another's wealth, or ill-will toward another, come and purify me? — that is, I purify all beings, but the sin that has gathered within me — it is only that pure man who can burn it away.

Thus the term of Gangaji's existence has indeed run out. Moreover, she herself is a widow; and it is for this reason that in our culture there is a custom of calling widowed women "Ganga-svarup." Yet in the Ganga Sahasranama, her 986th name is "Saubhagyasundari" — she who appears supremely beautiful through great good fortune — and her 974th name is "Strishu Saubhagyadayini" — she who bestows good fortune on women. Thus there are contradictory pronouncements regarding the Ganga.

Mokshapatrika, Registration no. 240, page 131, Samvat 1982, Issue 5, writes (Registration 242, p. 260):

_Gangaditirthavaryeshu dushtai re vavriteshviha,_
_Tirohitadhidaiveshu Krishna eva gatirmam. ||3||_
(When the finest of pilgrimage sites, such as the Ganga, have been overrun by wicked people, and their presiding divine power has become hidden, Krishna alone is my refuge.)

Shri Acharya Mahaprabhuji, four and a half centuries ago (Samvat 1532), says that because wicked people have come to dwell in the finest pilgrimage sites such as the Ganga, the divine power and glory of these sites has been lost. In such times, Shri Krishna alone is my refuge.

Mokshapatrika, Registration no. 242, page 147, writes: when the Lord Vamanji, in his manifest form, at the sacrifice of King Bali, took his great cosmic form, pressed down the earth with his right foot, and raised his left foot high, the nail of that foot's toe pierced the upper region of the universe, and a stream of water issued forth from it. This account suggests that Brahma's kamandal was overturned by the Lord's foot striking it. But this used, leftover water of the offering made by the Sanakadi sages, which was in the kamandal, could not have washed the Lord's foot. From this it can be said that Gangaji is nothing but the leftover water of Brahma's kamandal, which held the sweat of the Sanakadi sages — yet devotees of the Ganga are deceived by this Ganga, this Honest-Looking Thief.

Registration no. 445, page 836, lists the various Gangas: Bhagirathi, Mandakini, Alaknanda, Yamuna (a Himalayan river), Sheshaganga, Vishnuganga, Ramganga, Vyasganga, Karnaganga, Nandaganga, Garudganga, Virganga, Patalganga, Tungabhadra, and so on. There is also an Akashganga (celestial Ganga), and the river south of the Godavari is also called a Ganga.

Great, eminent sadhus and saints do indeed settle and dwell along the banks of the Ganga, but they do so in the hope of being purified by bathing in her — and for that reason they cannot be called "Harijan." As for who truly deserves the name Harijan, Jivanji Maharaj gives this sakhi:

_Karma hamaro katasi, koi harijan aave manhi,_
_Je kare hamari vasana, Jivana so to harijan nahin. ||15||_
(Hoping "our karma will be cut away if some Harijan comes and dwells within us" — whoever harbours this desire, O Jivan, is no Harijan at all.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: the Ganga and other pilgrimage sites hold the expectation that if someone comes and settles within them, their own karmic burden will be lightened; and one who nurtures such a hope cannot be called a Harijan, a true devotee who purifies us.

Gangaji, when preparing to descend to the earth, said to Bhagirath: "I am willing to fall upon the earth, but there must be some man capable of bearing my force; if there is no such person, I will split the earth open and plunge into the netherworld, and will not come upon the earth at all. For people wash away their own sins in me — but where, then, do I wash away my own impurity? Find a solution to this." Bhagirath replied: "Great souls who have renounced all attachment, who purify the world, who are tranquil, and who know the true nature of Brahman — such men will bathe in you and thereby destroy your sin, because within them dwells Shri Hari, the destroyer of sin; and Shankar, the very soul of all embodied beings, will bear the force of your descent." Having said this to the Ganga, the king began to please Shankar through austerities. In a short time Shankar became pleased, and, granting Bhagirath's request, received the Ganga — purified by the feet of Shri Hari — upon his own head.

Gangaji was proud of her own force, but Shivji humbled that pride. This is mentioned by Prabhudutt Brahmachari in his Bhagavati Katha, part 32, page 104:

_Gangane socha main shreshtha hun, kintu Shivjine unhe apni jataon mein dharan kiya, to Shivji shreshtha hue. Shivjiko bhi Kailas dharan karta hai, vah shreshtha hua. Kailashko Ravanne lilase utha liya, vah shreshtha hua. Ravanko Baline kankh mein daba liya, to vah shreshtha hua. Valiko bhi Bhagavanne ek banse mar diya. Is prakar dekhte hain, sansarmein Bhagavan ke atirikt koi yah nahin kah sakta ki ham sarva shreshtha hain._
(Ganga thought, "I am supreme" — but Shivji held her in his matted locks, so Shivji was supreme. Kailas bears Shivji, so Kailas was supreme. Ravana lifted Kailas playfully, so he was supreme. Vali pinned Ravana under his armpit, so he was supreme. But the Lord slew Vali with a single arrow. Thus we see that in this world none but the Lord himself can say, "I am supreme above all.")

Who is greatest, judged by benefit to the world, has been reckoned as follows:

_Sap kahai main bada, dharatiko uthaya. Shiv kahai main bada, maine tujhe galen mein dala. Ravan kahai main bada, maine Kailasko uthaya. Vali kahai main bada, maine tujhe haraya. Ram kahai main bada, maine tujhe mara. Sita kahai main badi, tum mere chakkarmein fasaya. Hanuman kahai main bada, mainne tumko hirdemein gada. Bharatji to bole nahin, Hanumantka tang toda. Guru hai bada Govindate._
(The serpent says, "I am great, I bear the earth." Shiva says, "I am great, I placed you around my neck." Ravana says, "I am great, I lifted Kailas." Vali says, "I am great, I defeated you." Ram says, "I am great, I slew you." Sita says, "I am great, I trapped you in my snare." Hanuman says, "I am great, I have fixed you within my heart." Bharatji, however, said nothing — yet he broke Hanuman's pride. The Guru is greater even than Govind.)

The pride of Gangaji was subdued by getting caught in the matted locks of Shivji. As the Ganga followed behind Bhagirath's chariot, she flooded the site prepared for the sage Jahnu's sacrifice; so Jahnu, in response, drank up the Ganga in a single sip. When Bhagirath pleaded, he released her from his ear, and so she came to be called Jahnavi. It is also said that at the time of her descent, as the Ganga was flowing toward the ocean, her meditation was disturbed, and she angrily swallowed the powerful rushing flow of water into her own thigh; then, at Bhagirath's prayer, she cut open her own thigh and released the Ganga out through that path — and so the Ganga is called Jahnavi, "daughter of the sage Jahnu." Moreover, this Ganga is the sweat-water of the Sanakadi sages, which Brahmaji had collected in his own kamandal; and so, in the Ganga Sahasranama, her name "Parameshthikamandalu" — she who dwells in Brahma's kamandal — and the name "Brahmadrav," meaning the Ganga, has further been given the name "Vishnupadodaki," water of Vishnu's feet, and an attempt has been made to mislead people, drawing them through deception into devotion to Vishnu — and this is the work of the Honest-Looking Thief. The Yajna has been declared to be a form of Vishnu; among the incarnations, the seventh is counted as the Yajna-Purusha, the sacrifice personified, and so the mantra "Yajno vai Vishnuh" (the sacrifice indeed is Vishnu) is found in texts such as the Taittiriya Brahmana, Aitareya Brahmana, Shatapatha Brahmana, Shankhayana Brahmana, and Taittiriya Samhita, among others — and Jivanji Maharaj has called the incarnations "Honest-Looking Thieves"; so this attempt to establish the Yajna, in the guise of the Yajna-Purusha, as devotion to Vishnu, is itself the work of this Honest-Looking Thief.

The procedure for performing the Ashwamedha sacrifice is an elaborate account of the attainment of pleasure and suffering.

Vaishnavji further said that even within devotion to Vishnu such a quarrel — of retaining worldly desires — has been set up that the soul cannot attain the Supreme Lord through it. There is also a second matter: that of the Ashwamedha sacrifice, through which too the soul cannot cross over. Its predicament: the horse must be white, with a garland of flowers around its neck, its tail yellow, its ears dark-coloured, on its left flank a mark shaped like a moringa leaf ("sejan"), its eyes red — this horse is to be brought forth, and twenty thousand Brahmins invited to the ceremony, their wives to be honoured alongside them as one honours a guru, and gifts given to them. Gifts to be given: one horse, one elephant, one bhar of gold (a bhar being about eight thousand rupees' weight), a thousand milch cows with their calves, one golden chariot, two hundred [units of] gems (one prasth being sixty-four rupees' weight) — this much as dakshina is to be given to each and every Brahmin. A golden plate is to be tied to the horse's head, on which is written: "If anyone is powerful enough, let him bind this horse; otherwise, worship it and set it free." Wherever the horse rolls on the ground, a lake is to be dug there; wherever it urinates, a well is to be dug; wherever it defecates, a stepwell is to be dug; wherever it stands still, a garden is to be planted; wherever it neighs, a place of free food-distribution is to be established. If, during all this, someone binds the horse, he must not be struck. If the horse goes into water, into fire, into the sky, or into the netherworld, one must follow it there as well. It roams fifty crore yojanas of the earth over twelve months, and until the horse returns after a full year, the king, the queens, and the officiating priest must not rise from their seats. For that entire year, until the horse returns, the fire-offering in the yajna must remain unbroken; the sacred fire must not be interrupted. After that, the horse is slain and offered to the thirty-three crore deities; it is killed and offered as an oblation in the sacrificial pit. One who performs a hundred such Ashwamedha sacrifices attains the throne of Indra. He enjoys the throne of Indra for one full cycle of the four ages, and for seventy-two such cycles. The hundred horses that are sacrificed are reborn as universal emperors, and other, lesser lives sacrificed daily are reborn as vassal kings — for as long as the ruler of the world continues to enjoy the throne of Indra.

Furthermore, when some other king on earth performs a hundred Ashwamedha sacrifices and ascends to the throne of Indra, the earlier king who had been enjoying that throne is told by the god of death, "O lord, your merit is now exhausted; go now to the mortal world" — and the new Indra arrives to claim the throne. When Indrani, along with the thirty-three crore deities, goes to receive the new king, the former king who had occupied the throne of Indra is seized by the toe of his left foot and cast down into the mortal world. Around Mount Mahendrachal there stands a thorny tree, like a silk-cotton tree but made of thunderbolt, called "Trimaliya"; it is spun about in reverse. There, the former Indra, cast down into the mortal world, becomes caught, lodged in the very midst of the tree. Then all the universal emperors and all the vassal kings who exist come there, and all of them are reborn as birds. Whichever weapon slew each of them becomes that bird's beak, made of thunderbolt, and all of them come and cling to the former king, pecking at him with their beaks. The king cries out in great anguish, and no one comes to free him. As for how long this state continues, there is this statement from Adhyaruji's Vedapuran:

_Jagan danadik raj prapat hoe, dharam khutene vali dukh seh e._
(Through sacrifice and the giving of gifts one obtains kingship, but once one's merit runs out, one must once again endure suffering.)

Kalyan, Year, Issue no. 3, page 739, Registration no. 19, writes:

_Vedonki mul samhitaonmein na to badi badi yajnonka vidhi vidhan hai aur na darshanik gutthiyan hi suljhachi gachi hai. Vahan to rishijan bilkul sidhe-sade dhangse Bhagavanki stuti karte nazar aate hain._
(In the root Samhitas of the Vedas there is neither an ordinance prescribing grand sacrifices, nor are philosophical knots untangled there. There, the sages appear simply praising God in a plain, straightforward manner.)

This is a very beautiful passage.

Thus, for seventy-two cycles — that is, 288 ages — he remained caught in that tree and suffered greatly. Whatever kingdom he had ruled, that much suffering he must endure. Furthermore, when the next holder of Indra's throne arrives, whichever former Indra is caught in the tree at that time is cast down into the mortal world; he then endures eighty-four lakh species of rebirth.

_Jalja nav lakshani dash lakshani pakshinah,_
_Trishallakshan gavasyadya sthavaranancha vishantim,_
_Kramayo rudra lakshani chaturlakshani manavah,_
_Koti janme tu samprapte nridebo durlabhastatha. ||78||_
(Nine lakh species born in water, ten lakh species of birds, thirty lakh cow-and-kindred creatures, twenty lakh immobile species, eleven lakh crawling insects, and four lakh human beings — only after crores of such births are gone through does one obtain the rare human body.)

Of beings born in water there are nine lakh species; ten lakh species of birds; thirty lakh species of cows and the like; twenty lakh species of immobile beings; eleven lakh species of crawling insects; and four lakh human beings — among these, only after passing through crores of such births does one obtain the rare human body.

The Gita, chapter 9, verse 21, says:

_Te tam bhuktva svargalokam vishalam_
_kshine punye martyalokam vishanti,_
_Evam trayidharmamanupraapanna_
_gatagatam kamakama labhante. ||21||_
(Having enjoyed that vast heavenly realm, when their merit is exhausted, they enter the mortal world once more; thus those who follow the threefold Vedic path, desiring the objects of desire, obtain only a repeated coming and going.)

Having enjoyed that vast heavenly realm, when their merit runs out, they attain the human world once more — thus, those who take refuge in the desire-driven path of the Vedas, and who long for sense-objects, merely come and go again and again.

The Bhagavat, canto 11, chapter 10, verse 26, says:

_Tavat pramodate svarge, yavat punyam samapyate,_
_Kshinapunyah patatyarva ganichchhan kalachalitah. ||26||_
(He enjoys pleasure in heaven only until his merit is exhausted; then, his merit spent, driven by time, he falls back down against his will.)

As long as his merit is not exhausted, that meritorious man goes on enjoying pleasure in this way; then, when his merit runs out, driven onward by time, he falls back down, even though he has no wish to do so.

(A kavit-rekhta:)

_Nav lakh jalmein jiv, das pankhi parvara, ektalis lakh kramkit,_
_Vis sathavar vistara, char lakh manakh vadhani tattvaveta trihi,_
_Lokmein char lakh sacharachar, sab jivanmein dhanya jiv hai je samer dharani dhara._
(Nine lakh beings live in water, ten lakh among the birds, forty-one lakh crawling insects, twenty lakh spread among the immobile species, and four lakh forms of humankind, so say the knowers of truth. In the world there are, in all, eighty-four lakh species of the moving and unmoving — and among all living beings, blessed is that being who bears the burden of the earth.)

The original Samagam's pages 305-306 are missing; on what remains of page 306, the last half of verse 78 reads as follows: "...ti divyamana tam eva sharanagata" — meaning: O Supreme Being of divine radiance, your devotees come to your refuge. The commentary on this verse is as follows:

Commentary: those nine lakh forms of incarnation in water, ten lakh forms as birds, eleven lakh forms as crawling insects, thirty lakh forms as immobile beings, twenty (thirty) lakh forms as cows and other such creatures, and four lakh forms as human beings — through these, by chance, one may be born, attain a kingdom and enjoy it; may perform sacrifices; may ascend to the throne of Indra; may again become lodged in the tree; may again fall to the mortal world — these are the entanglements, the hardships one wanders through. But having gone through all this, if one comes to take refuge in a Guru, then all karma is dispelled. This is the 46th verse of the Pandava Gita:

_Go kotidanam grahaneshu Kashiprayaga-Gangayutakalpavasah,_
_Yajnayutam meru-suvarnadanam Govindanamna na kadapi tulyam. ||79||_
(The gift of crores of cows during an eclipse, ten thousand kalpas of residence at Kashi, Prayag, and on the banks of the Ganga, ten thousand sacrifices, and the gift of gold equal to Mount Meru — none of this can ever equal the name of Govind.)

The gift of crores of cows at the time of an eclipse, ten thousand kalpas of dwelling at Kashi, Prayag, and the banks of the Ganga, ten thousand yajnas, and the gift of gold equal in weight to Mount Meru — all of this together can never equal the one name of the Supreme Lord.

(Parashuram's kavit:)

_Kapil dhen jaltar, kot jo Ganga tirath nahave,_
_Vipra taran pargar, pokh de bhalo manave,_
_De gaj gahvar dan, bhom dohari manave,_
_Kanak patra de soparna, chir tokha pahanave,_
_Ashvamegh jagan kare, kot kanya parnave,_
_Turi aan palan, khandh de aap chadave,_
_Kiyo na mite Keshava, Farasram Govind bin._
(Even if one worships the tawny cow, bathes in the waters of crores of Ganga pilgrimage sites, washes the feet of Brahmins and lovingly provides for their nourishment, secretly gives away elephants in charity, gives gifts of land, gives golden plates and jewelled ornaments, dresses recipients in fine bright garments, performs the Ashwamedha sacrifice, gives away crores of maidens in marriage, brings a fine horse fully saddled and mounts and offers it himself — Parashuram says, O Keshava, none of this deed is undone without devotion to Govind.)

Parashuram says: one who worships the dusky-hued cow, bathes in the waters of crores of pilgrimage sites of the Ganga, washes the feet of Brahmins and takes delight in nourishing them well, secretly gives away elephants in charity, gives away two pieces of land, gives gold-plated gifts and dresses recipients in bright garments, performs the Ashwamedha sacrifice, gives away crores of maidens in marriage, brings the full trappings for a horse and mounts and decorates it himself and gives it away — even so, whatever deeds one has done, without devotion to God, however many such religious observances one performs, deliverance will not come.

_Dayala Harki ehi van hai, je harijanke bas hoy,_
_Kot jagan jo koi karo, pan harijan tyan Hari hoy. ||10||_
(Merciful is this word spoken by Hari himself — that he remains under the sway of his devotees; even if someone performs crores of sacrifices, Hari still dwells only wherever his true devotees are.)

This is a word spoken by God's own mouth: that he remains under the control of his Harijans; therefore, even if someone performs crores of sacrifices, God remains present only where his Harijans, his devotees, are.

The fruit of one's merit cannot be erased even by Keshav-Krishna himself. Therefore the merit earned through giving cows, pilgrimage, gifts to Brahmins, the Ashwamedha sacrifice, the gift of maidens, and the like, cannot be erased — it must be experienced. But if instead you sing the praises and glories of Govind, such a result will not come about.

Kabirji stirred up a revolution against the forces that deceive and disrupt devotion to Vishnu through fraud, but nothing came of it in the end. Yet our true Guru, Jivanji, without holding back out of shame, boldly and courageously exposed these forces, and it is this exposure that has been presented in this Samagam. It has shown how the soul is prevented from crossing over by the confusion of maya and Brahma:

1. Through the confusion of maya and Brahma, the soul cannot cross over.
2. Through the thirteen-and-a-half kandas of the Yajurveda, there remains a confusion between devotion and liberation, so the soul cannot attain the Supreme Lord.
3. The unbroken divine play of Vasudev cannot be perceived, through the Guru's grace, by one who has not attained it.
4. Jivanji came for the welfare and salvation of the soul.
5. "If one, freed from the bondage of the three states caused by the three gunas — birth, death, and old age — worships Me, one attains the nectar of My liberation and is delivered."
6. Unless one is freed from the deception of the ten incarnations, the soul cannot attain the Supreme Lord.
7. Without devotion to Vishnu, the Supreme Reality cannot be attained; the eighty-eight thousand sages, the thirty-three crore deities, and Brahma and others are all turned away from Vasudev, hostile to devotion to Vishnu — the righteousness of Govind will not appear to them.
8. In Aryavarta, in the Kali age, such Vaishnavas will appear that, through the sarshti kind of liberation set in motion by the Sanakadi sages across the three ages, they will attain power and majesty equal to God's own.
9. Vaishnavji revealed the path of liberation-while-living.
10. Unless the true form of a saint is understood, how can one attain the Supreme Lord?
11. If the Honest-Looking Thief keeps circling around one's devotion to Vishnu, the soul cannot cross over.
12. The quarrel that has been set up over the Ashwamedha and similar rites, within devotion to Vishnu, prevents the soul from attaining the Supreme Lord.
13. Finally, it was explained that if the great entanglements — the hardships and obstructions caused by the thief within devotion to Vishnu — are released, then the soul attains the Supreme Lord in this way.

The Honest-Looking Thieves described in the Samagam have been written about in the sakhis of the Garbhavali section.

_Aap vyapak Jivana, tej jot kiya akas,_
_Bin mundka chor hai, sab jag kiya garas. ||3||_
(Self-pervading, O Jivan, Brahman made itself into radiance, light, and sky; this headless thief has devoured the entire world.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: Brahma-radiance, Brahma-light, and the five great elements — fire, light, sky, and the rest — this spontaneous self-pervasion of the unqualified Brahman occurs of its own accord. This Brahman is like a headless thief, a thief without form, and it has swallowed up, devoured, the entire world.

_Aatam parmeshvar pame nahi, Jivana keha vichar,_
_Shahutor aage fire, sohi bade vatpar. ||4||_
(The soul does not attain the Supreme Lord, O Jivan — such is my reflection; whatever keeps circling in front as an "Honest-Looking Thief" — that indeed is the greatest highway robber.)

Devotees, terrified of these wicked thieves, ask Jivandasji Maharaj: O Jivandasji, such cunning thieves of maya have kept circling before our devotion — they alone are the great robbers, and because of them the soul cannot attain the Supreme Being. So please tell us who these thieves are, and what they are like.

_Pahela dash avatar hai, duja Vaikuntha jan,_
_Trijo Omkar Jivana, chotha ghatghat man. ||5||_
(The first is the ten incarnations; know the second to be Vaikuntha; the third, O Jivan, is Omkar; and the fourth is the notion that God is fully present in every single vessel.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: the first Honest-Looking Thief is the ten incarnations; know that the second is Vaikuntha; the third is Omkar; and the fourth thief is the claim that the Supreme Brahman is fully and completely present in every single heart — this too, understand, is a Honest-Looking Thief, as I have told you.

_Panchman Sanakadik hai, chhathi Bhagirathi Ganga,_
_Satmi Ekadashi Jivana, jivkun baura kin. ||6||_
(The fifth is the Sanakadi sages, the sixth is the Bhagirathi Ganga, and the seventh, O Jivan, is Ekadashi — which has driven every living being mad and bewildered.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: the fifth Honest-Looking Thief is the Sanakadi sages, the sixth is the Bhagirathi Ganga, and the seventh is Ekadashi — which has made all living beings mad and utterly bewildered.

_Sat Vishnu bhakti manhi mile, apane pad lai jay,_
_Mota odavada Jivana, Parmeshvar nahi pay. ||7||_
(These seven mingle within devotion to Vishnu, and lead one away to their own respective abodes; great are these entanglements, O Jivan — through them one does not attain the Supreme Lord.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: all these Honest-Looking Thieves mix themselves in under the name of devotion to Vishnu, and then lead us away, each to its own abode; therefore all of them are great entanglements — troubles that, like the trailing end of a sari catching on things, cloak the true practice of devotion to Vishnu with their perverse influence.

_Sapt shahuchor taje, tab Vishnu bhakti ja hoy,_
_Tab hi aatam Jivana, male param pad soy. ||8||_
(Only when one abandons these seven Honest-Looking Thieves does true devotion to Vishnu come about; only then, O Jivan, does the soul attain that supreme state.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: only when one renounces these seven Honest-Looking Thieves can true devotion to Vishnu come about, and only then can the soul attain that true supreme state, the abode of God.

Selfish, cunning thieves infiltrate devotion to Vishnu by deceiving people, joining in through guerrilla-like methods, and corrupt our devotion from within — these thieves have been exposed by Jivanji Maharaj, and he has made us alert so that we may be saved from them. It is written in the Samagam that Jivandasji therefore said: "O brothers, walk with your eyes open — these are the Honest-Looking Thieves of devotion to Vishnu" — and this account has been given, beginning with the first, the ten incarnations, and so on, as Jivandasji
